'''Theodore Kuwana''' (1931–2022) was a chemist and academic researcher known as the founding father of the field of [[spectroelectrochemistry]].  

Kuwana's academic career included appointments at [[California Institute of Technology]], the [[University of California, Riverside]], [[Case Western Reserve University|Case Institute of Technology]], [[Ohio State University]], and finally at the [[University of Kansas]]. At KU, he was Regents Distinguished Professor of Chemistry and Pharmaceutical Chemistry, the Director of the Center for Bioanalytical Research, and Emeritus Distinguished Professor. He served as managing director of the [[Analytical Sciences Digital Library]].  

During his career, Kuwana mentored more than 70 graduate students. 

== Early life and education ==
[[File:Kuwana-family.jpg|left|thumb|Kuwana family. Theodore is at bottom, center.]]
Theodore Kuwana, a son of Japanese immigrant (''[[Issei]]'') parents Yoshino and Nenokichi Kuwana, was born August 3, 1931, in [[Idaho Falls, Idaho]], in the United States.<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 23, 1940 |title=1940 United States Federal Census |url=https://www.ancestry.com/imageviewer/collections/2442/images/M-T0627-00741-00693?pId=99626410 |url-access=subscription |access-date=May 10, 2023 |website= |via=ancestry.com}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Remembering the life of Theodore Kuwana, PhD |url=https://obituaries.seattletimes.com/obituary/theodore-kuwana-phd-1084324648/ |access-date=2023-05-10 |website=obituaries.seattletimes.com |language=en}}</ref> 

Kuwana wrote, "I was the youngest of six children; my parents were immigrant [[Tenant farmer|tenant potato farmers]]... When I was 10 and 12, I lost my father and mother, respectively, to cancer. Early on, mother had said, 'You must go to college.' I was the only one in our family to do so."<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Kuwana |first1=Ted |last2=Kuwana |first2=Jane |date=Dec 2022 |title=A path of luck and light |journal=Electroanalysis |language=en |volume=34 |issue=12 |pages=1821–1822 |doi=10.1002/elan.202200008 |issn=1040-0397|doi-access=free }}</ref> His interest in chemistry started while he was in elementary school, when he was given a [[A. C. Gilbert Company|Gilbert]] [[chemistry set]] one Christmas. In high school he won the [[Bausch & Lomb]] Medal for Excellence in chemistry.<ref name=":1" /> 

Kuwana's baccalaureate degree in 1954 was from [[Antioch College]] where with R.G. Yalman he published his first research article in a major journal.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yalman |first1=Richard G. |last2=Kuwana |first2=Theodore |date=Apr 1955 |title=Properties of Acidocobaltammines. III. cis-Nitritotetrammines |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry |language=en |volume=59 |issue=4 |pages=298–300 |doi=10.1021/j150526a005 |issn=0022-3654}}</ref> His M.S. in 1956 was from [[Cornell University]].<ref name=":2" /> Kuwana earned his Ph.D. in 1959 at the [[University of Kansas]], with a dissertation titled, ''Studies in Electroanalytical Chemistry: The Development of a Mercury Chloride Film Anode and Chronopotentiometric Studies in Aqueous and Non-aqueous Solutions,'' supervised by [[Ralph N. Adams]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=1959 |title=T Kuwana - 1959 - University of Kansas, Chemistry |url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&as_sdt=0,38&q=%22Studies+in+Electroanalytical+chemistry+:+the+development+of+a+mercury+chloride+film+anode+and+chronopotentiometric+studies+in+aqueous+and+non-aqueous+solutions%22&btnG= |access-date=2023-05-10 |website=scholar.google.com}}</ref>

In 1965, Kuwana wed Jane Bader.<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 2, 1965 |title=Miss Jane Bader is Bride of Mr. Kuwana |page=5 |work=[[Iowa City Press-Citizen]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/iowa-city-press-citizen-miss-jane-bader/124385222/ |access-date=2023-05-10 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> Because she understood the chemistry and was also a talented writer and editor, she edited his writings. The couple had a son, a daughter, and four granddaughters.<ref name=":2" />

== Career ==
After postdoctoral training with Fred Anson at [[California Institute of Technology]], Kuwana briefly worked at an aerospace firm<ref name=":1" /> before he went to the [[University of California, Riverside]], in 1960 as a visiting assistant professor.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Emeritus Distinguished Professor Theodore ''Ted'' Kuwana: August 3, 1931 - January 1, 2022 |url=https://chem.ku.edu/emeritus-distinguished-professor-theodore-ted-kuwana-august-3-1931-january-1-2022 |access-date=2023-05-10 |website=chem.ku.edu |date=January 24, 2022 |language=en}}</ref> He became an associate professor at Case Institute of Technology (now [[Case Western Reserve University]]) in 1965, and a full professor there in 1968. From 1971–1986 he was on the faculty of [[Ohio State University]]. Kuwana joined the faculty at the [[University of Kansas]] in 1986, becoming Regents Distinguished Professor of Chemistry and Pharmaceutical Chemistry, and the Director of the Center for Bioanalytical Research.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Former OSU Professor, Founding Father of Spectroelectrochemistry, Ted Kuwana Passed Away {{!}} Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry |url=https://chemistry.osu.edu/news/former-osu-professor-founding-father-spectroelectrochemistry-ted-kuwana-passed-away |access-date=2023-05-10 |website=chemistry.osu.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Kuwana is recognized as the founding father of [[spectroelectrochemistry]]:<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Heineman |first1=William R. |last2=Winograd |first2=Nicholas |last3=Jensen |first3=William B. |date=Dec 2022 |title=Spectroelectrochemistry Using Optically Transparent Electrodes – Ted Kuwana and the Early Years |journal=Electroanalysis |language=en |volume=34 |issue=12 |pages=1826–1833 |doi=10.1002/elan.202100493 |s2cid=240601492 |issn=1040-0397 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wilson |first=George S. |date=Dec 2022 |title=Spectroelectrochemistry of Proteins |journal=Electroanalysis |language=en |volume=34 |issue=12 |pages=1834–1841 |doi=10.1002/elan.202100535 |s2cid=243840919 |issn=1040-0397}}</ref> 

{{Blockquote|text=The origin of spectroelectrochemistry at an OTE [optically transparent electrode] appears to date from a conversation held at the University of Kansas in the late 1950's between young assistant professor Ralph Adams and his first graduate student Ted Kuwana. As recalled by Kuwana, Adams, while observing the production of an intense yellow color in the solution near a platinum [[anode]] during the oxidation of [[o-tolidine]] commented that "...it would be nice to have a 'see through' electrode to spectrally identify the colored species being formed..." Later, Kuwana obtained samples of a conducting glass ([[antimony]] doped tin oxide-coated glass), and the first spectroelectrochemistry at an OTE was performed on o-tolidine.|author=William R. Heineman<ref>{{Cite web |last=Heineman |first=William R. |title=Spectroelectrochemistry at Optically Transparent Electrodes: An Historical Perspective |url=https://www.electrochem.org/dl/ma/201/pdfs/1301.pdf}}</ref>}}
{{Blockquote|text=Now equipped with a "see through" electrode, Kuwana and his students used these conducting glass OTEs for the first spectroelectrochemical experiments of electrogenerated solution species. Graduate student Keith Darlington and undergraduate student Don Leedy performed the experiments using o-tolidine, a colorless compound that undergoes a 2-electron oxidation to form an intensely yellow colored species – the very reaction that Kuwana studied as a graduate student at Kansas that sparked Adams' prophetic comment. They monitored formation of the yellow species at 437 nm using a constant anodic current (i. e., chronopotentiometry – a technique that was more commonly used at the time than it is now) and reported the results in their classic 1964 paper.|author=William R. Heineman, Nicholas Winograd, William B. Jensen<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Heineman |first1=William R. |last2=Winograd |first2=Nicholas |last3=Jensen |first3=William B. |date=Dec 2022 |title=Spectroelectrochemistry Using Optically Transparent Electrodes – Ted Kuwana and the Early Years |journal=Electroanalysis |language=en |volume=34 |issue=12 |pages=1826–1833 |doi=10.1002/elan.202100493 |s2cid=240601492 |issn=1040-0397}}</ref>}}
Describing Kuwana's "profound impact on [[analytical chemistry]] education", Wenzel, ''et al.'', wrote that Kuwana set up a series of workshops with industrial leaders to evaluate the undergraduate analytical sciences curriculum and design improvements. The main recommendation from the workshop participants was that "the undergraduate analytical sciences curriculum needed to engage students in problem-based experiences in the classroom and laboratory portion of courses."<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Wenzel |first1=Thomas J. |last2=Kelly |first2=Richard S. |last3=Larive |first3=Cynthia K. |last4=Gross |first4=Erin M. |date=Dec 2022 |title=Contributions of Ted Kuwana to Analytical Sciences Education |journal=Electroanalysis |language=en |volume=34 |issue=12 |pages=1823–1825 |doi=10.1002/elan.202100250 |s2cid=237841844 |issn=1040-0397|doi-access=free |url=https://escholarship.org/content/qt82w3c4nt/qt82w3c4nt.pdf?t=r9azxy }}</ref> 

The workshop participants also recommended a digital library of resources and links to resources for instructors designing [[problem-based learning]] for lectures and laboratories. Kuwana partnered with the [[American Chemical Society]], Division of [[Analytical chemistry|Analytical Chemistry]], to set up a partnership for educational outreach. The [[Analytical Sciences Digital Library]] (ASDL) was formed, and it was supported with funding from the [[National Science Foundation]].<ref name=":4" /> Kuwana served as managing director. Editor [[Cynthia Larive]] acknowledged "the leadership and continued contributions of Professor Emeritus Ted Kuwana, University of Kansas, to the development and continued evolution of the ASDL project".<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Larive |first=Cynthia K. |date=2009 |title=The Analytical Sciences Digital Library (ASDL) |journal=Anal Bioanal Chem |volume=395 |issue=8 |pages=2425–2429 |doi=10.1007/s00216-009-3226-6|s2cid=37541802 |pmc=2780681 }}</ref>[[File:Susan Lunte, Ted Kuwana.jpg|thumb|Ted Kuwana in lab with [[Susan M. Lunte]]]]According to Richard L. McCreery, "Ted Kuwana was not only a scientific leader in [[electrochemistry]] and related fields, but he was also an excellent citizen and unselfish contributor to the careers of many other scientists, myself included."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=McCreery |first=Richard L. |date=Dec 2022 |title=Ted Kuwana as a Senior Colleague, Mentor and Scientific Leader |journal=Electroanalysis |language=en |volume=34 |issue=12 |pages=1842–1843 |doi=10.1002/elan.202100538 |s2cid=241739370 |issn=1040-0397}}</ref> Over his career, Kuwana advised and mentored 73 graduate students.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Chemistry Tree Children - Theodore Kuwana |url=https://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=68694 |access-date=2023-05-11 |website=academictree.org}}</ref>

Kuwana died of pneumonia in [[Seattle]] on January 1, 2022, at age 90 years.<ref name=":2" />

* [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research Foundation Lifetime Achievement Award (2002)<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR) |url=https://new.nsf.gov/funding/initiatives/epscor |access-date=2023-05-12 |website=National Science Foundation}}</ref>
